events.text: An old monk sweeping the temple steps stops when you pass. The broom goes still. "Ah," the monk says, as if greeting a neighbour back from the market. "You again. The last time, you were taller. The time before, you owed me a bowl of rice." Nobody else on the steps seems to find this strange.

choices.text: Bow, and ask what you owed

effects.log: "A bowl of rice and an apology," the monk says. "You may pay the rice. The apology can wait. It has waited many lives."

choices.text: Laugh it off and walk on

effects.log: You laugh. The monk laughs too, exactly the same laugh as yours. That is the strange part.

choices.text: Sit on the steps and listen

effects.log: The monk talks about weather from years nobody alive remembers. Every word of it sounds right.

events.text: The monk is waiting at the temple gate with two bowls of rice. "Eat," the monk says. "Then tell me which of your lives you liked best. Everyone who keeps coming back has a favourite. Most of them lie about it."

choices.text: Tell the truth: the one with the quiet life

effects.log: The monk nods slowly. "The quiet ones are always the favourite. Nobody ever says the glorious ones."

choices.text: Say this one. It is the only one you have

effects.log: "Good answer," the monk says. "Wrong, but good." The rice is excellent.

choices.text: Ask which life the monk liked best

effects.log: The monk thinks a long time. "The one where you planted the pear tree by the gate." There is a pear tree by the gate.

events.text: The monk is very old now, and lying in a small room that smells of incense and pears. "I do not come back," the monk says. "I chose that, a long time ago. You chose differently. Neither of us was wrong." A thin hand points at a box under the bed.

choices.text: Open the box

effects.log: Inside: a pill, wrapped in paper, and a note in your own hand from another life: Give this back to me. When the monk had kept it is anyone's guess.

choices.text: Hold the hand until the end

effects.log: The monk goes quietly, smiling at something above your shoulder. You sweep the temple steps that evening. The broom fits your hands.

choices.text: Promise to find the monk next life

effects.log: "Do not," the monk says, very kindly. "Some people you only meet once. That is what makes them precious."

events.text: A monk you have never met pours you tea at a roadside shrine and pushes the cup across. "You drink it too fast," the monk says. "You always did. Life after life, and you still drink tea as if someone will take it away."

choices.text: Drink it slowly, this once

effects.log: Slowly, it tastes of smoke and pine. You realise you have never once tasted tea properly.

choices.text: Ask how the monk knows the number

effects.log: "I count the cups," the monk says, and refills yours. It is not an answer. You accept it.

choices.text: Drink it fast, out of spite

effects.log: The monk laughs so hard the shrine bell rings by itself.

events.text: At a great temple, the abbot comes out to the gate in full ceremonial robes and bows to you, low, before a hundred watching monks. "This one," the abbot says, "has been born more times than this temple has stood. Learn from them." Then, more quietly: "Please do not make a speech."

choices.text: Return the bow, exactly as low

effects.log: Two bows, equal. The monks talk about it for years. Nobody can say who bowed first.

choices.text: Make a very short speech

effects.log: "Eat when you are hungry. Sleep when you are tired. Do it again." The abbot looks relieved.

choices.text: Ask to sweep the steps instead

effects.log: You sweep the thousand steps in silence. By the bottom, you understand something you have been missing for a hundred lives.

events.text: A crossroads in {echo_region}: four roads, a stone marker, a crooked willow. Your feet stop on their own. You have never been here. Your heart is pounding as if you are about to die. You know, the way you know your own name, that you once did. Here. Of {echo_cause}.

choices.text: Take the left road, as that life did not

effects.log: You take the left road. Nothing happens. The relief is so great you laugh out loud alone on the road.

choices.text: Stand still until the feeling passes

effects.log: It takes until dusk. When it passes, it leaves behind a calm you did not have this morning.

choices.text: Touch the stone marker

effects.log: There is a nick in the stone at hand height. Your fingers fit it exactly.

events.text: You dream of the crossroads every night now. In the dream it is always raining, and someone is always waiting under the willow, and you never reach them in time. A fortune teller in the market takes one look at you and refuses your coin.

choices.text: Go back to the crossroads in the rain

ok.log: Rain, the willow, nobody waiting. You stand where you died and say, out loud, that it is over. The dreams stop.

fail.log: You catch a fever standing in the rain like a fool. The dreams keep coming, but they are softer now.

choices.text: Ask the fortune teller why

effects.log: "I do not read the dead," the fortune teller says, "and half of you is still lying at that crossroads."

choices.text: Stay awake to keep the dream away

effects.log: Three nights without sleep. On the fourth, the dream comes anyway, and this time you are a little closer.

events.text: The willow at the crossroads has been cut down. A tea stall stands there now, and the tea seller says the old tree fell in a storm. Under the stump, the roots have grown around something: a small stone, carved with a name you once had.

choices.text: Take the stone with you

effects.log: It sits warm in your pocket. You never dream of the crossroads again.

choices.text: Leave it, and buy a cup of tea there

effects.log: The tea is good. You drink it where you died, and it is just a place now. A good place for tea.

choices.text: Plant a new willow over it

effects.log: You plant the sapling yourself. The tea seller promises to water it. Next life, maybe, it will give you shade.

events.text: You walk into a roadside inn you have never seen and go straight to the corner table without thinking. The innkeeper brings a pot of exactly the tea you like, unasked, then frowns. "Strange. I thought you were a regular. My grandmother's regular."

choices.text: Ask about the grandmother's regular

effects.log: Always the corner table. Always this tea. Died young, owing for a week of rooms. You pay the old debt. The innkeeper is baffled.

choices.text: Say you must have one of those faces

effects.log: "You do," the innkeeper says. "An old face. On a young person."

choices.text: Drink the tea and say nothing

effects.log: Some things are not for explaining. The tea is perfect, which proves it.

events.text: On a mountain path you have never climbed, you step aside a moment before a rock falls exactly where you were. Then again, an hour later, at a rotten plank. Your body is remembering a road that killed you, step by step, and walking it better this time.

choices.text: Let your body lead, and see where it goes

effects.log: It leads you around every danger and to a ledge with a view you once died trying to reach. It was worth it, then and now.

choices.text: Turn back. One death here was enough

effects.log: You go down slowly. Wisdom, you decide, is mostly knowing which roads to stop walking.

choices.text: Mark every danger for other travellers

effects.log: You leave white stones at every bad step. Years later, travellers call it the Path of the Careful Ghost.

events.text: A grave-keeper in {echo_region} squints at you, then at a list in a bamboo case. "There is a row up the hill," the grave-keeper says, "all different names, all different years, and every one of them was buried with that same look on their face. Yours. The newest is {echo_name}."

choices.text: Walk up the hill to the row

effects.log: Many stones in a line, different names, different deaths. You count them twice. You do not read them all. Not yet.

choices.text: Ask who paid for them

effects.log: "Each one paid for the one before," the grave-keeper says. "You always leave a little silver here. Habit."

choices.text: Pay the keeper to look after them

effects.log: "You always do that too," the grave-keeper says, pocketing it. (-15 taels)

events.text: You come back to the row of graves alone. Up close, the stones tell a story nobody else could read: young, old, young, very young, old. A sword carved on one, a ladle on another, a brush on a third. You were a cook once. You were good at it.

choices.text: Light incense at every stone

effects.log: It takes an hour. By the last stone the smoke hangs over the whole row like a single long breath.

choices.text: Sit by the youngest one

effects.log: Nine years old, the stone says. You tell that child about everything that came after. It was a lot.

choices.text: Study the sword carved on one

effects.log: Your hand moves along the carving and finishes a technique you have never learned. You practise it all evening.

events.text: The grave-keeper is waiting with a blank stone already cut and set at the end of the row. "For this one," the keeper says. "No hurry. We just like to be ready, with you."

choices.text: Carve your own name on it, now

effects.log: Your name, and no dates. It is a strange freedom, to see it there and walk away.

choices.text: Ask them to leave it blank

effects.log: "Blank, then," the keeper agrees. "For whoever you turn out to be."

choices.text: Laugh until you have to sit down

effects.log: The keeper laughs too. Two people laughing in a graveyard at a blank stone. It is the best afternoon of the year.

events.text: An old battlefield, grown over with wildflowers. You know three places in it where you have died, in three different wars, on three different sides. The flowers do not care which side. Neither, standing here, do you.

choices.text: Walk to each of the three places

effects.log: At each place you stand a while. By the third, the wars blur together into one long mistake.

choices.text: Pick flowers for all the dead here

effects.log: Your arms full, you lay them in the middle of the field. All sides, all wars, all of you.

choices.text: Train here, where you fell

effects.log: You practise the forms of all three lives at once. Something in your stance mends.

events.text: Pilgrims have started to come to a hillside where a hundred nameless graves stand in a ring. The story goes that one soul lies in all of them. Monks pray there for patience. You walk into the middle of the ring, and every pilgrim falls silent.

choices.text: Tell them the story is true

effects.log: Nobody believes you, and everybody does. By nightfall the ring has a new name. It is yours.

choices.text: Pray with the pilgrims, quietly

effects.log: You pray for patience beside your own graves. The pilgrims never know. It is better that way.

choices.text: Plant a pine in the middle of the ring

effects.log: The pine will outlive this life and the next one. Something of yours should stay put for once.

events.text: A small child in a village lane drops a ball, stares at you, and bursts into tears. "You promised!" the child shouts. "You promised you would come back for the kite festival!" The child's mother is mortified. You have never been to this village. Three lives ago, though, you made a promise.

choices.text: Kneel and ask about the promise

effects.log: A kite, a red one with a long tail, and a festival you never reached. The child tells it like yesterday.

choices.text: Apologise to the mother and leave

effects.log: You leave. The child's crying follows you to the end of the lane and much further.

choices.text: Say you are sorry you were late

effects.log: The child stops crying at once. "You are always late," the child says, very seriously.

events.text: The kite festival is next month. The child has drawn the kite from memory: a red carp with a long tail. Your hands know the frame before you touch the bamboo. The child's family watches you both with growing unease.

choices.text: Build the kite exactly as drawn

effects.log: It takes four evenings. It is the kite from the drawing, perfect, and you have never built a kite in this life.

choices.text: Explain to the family, honestly

ok.log: The grandmother listens, nods, and says a soul that keeps its promises across lives is welcome at her table.

fail.log: They do not believe a word. They let you build the kite anyway, under watch.

choices.text: Teach the child to build it

effects.log: Small hands, slow work, many broken struts. This time the kite will be the child's, not a promise.

events.text: Festival day. The red carp climbs higher than any kite on the hill. The child holds the string and laughs, and then, in the middle of the laugh, looks at you as if waking from a dream. "Who are you?" the child asks. The memory is gone. Only the kite is left.

choices.text: Say you are a friend of the child's

effects.log: "Oh," the child says, and goes back to the kite. A promise kept is allowed to be forgotten.

choices.text: Say nothing and watch it fly

effects.log: You watch until the sun goes down. Three lives late, and exactly on time.

choices.text: Give the child your own name to keep

effects.log: The child repeats the name twice and forgets it by dinner. Some day, another life, someone will shout it at you in a lane.

events.text: At a junk stall you find a little wooden horse with one ear missing. You know where the other ear is: you bit it off, teething, in a life where someone who loved you carved it. The stall keeper wants three taels.

choices.text: Buy it (3 taels)

effects.log: You carry it in your sleeve for the rest of this life. It weighs nothing and it is the heaviest thing you own. (-3 taels)

choices.text: Ask who sold it to the stall

effects.log: A family clearing an old house. A name you do not know, and know.

choices.text: Leave it for another child

effects.log: A toddler grabs it before you have turned around. That is where it belongs.

events.text: Thunder on a clear day, and a voice inside it, very weary: "You. Again. Do you know how much paperwork a soul makes, coming back again and again?" A small cloud lowers itself over your head and stays there, raining only on you.
events.arc: The Heavens Are Tired of You

choices.text: Apologise to the sky

effects.log: The cloud rains a little less. The heavens, it seems, are not used to apologies.

choices.text: Say you will keep coming back

effects.log: A long, tired rumble. "We know," the sky says. "That is the problem."

choices.text: Open your mouth and drink the rain

effects.log: Heaven's rain tastes faintly of ink. The cloud seems offended and follows you all day.

events.text: A clerk of the heavens comes down in person: an official in grey robes with an ink-stained sleeve and a scroll longer than a river. "Your file," the clerk says. "We need to discuss your file." Villagers pretend not to see the official standing on a cloud.
events.arc: The Heavens Are Tired of You

choices.text: Ask to read your file

ok.log: You read three lives before the clerk snatches it back. You learn more from them than from any manual.

fail.log: The writing moves when you look at it. The clerk sighs and rolls it up.

choices.text: Offer to help with the paperwork

effects.log: The clerk stares. Nobody has offered before. You spend a strange afternoon sorting cloud forms.

choices.text: Ask why they do not just stop you

effects.log: "Stop you?" The clerk looks genuinely shocked. "Returning is your right. Complaining about it is ours."

events.text: The clerk comes back with a stamp. "Approved," the clerk says, stamping the air above your head. "Your next return is pre-filed. Saves us all time. Try to die of something simple this time. Old age is very easy to process."
events.arc: The Heavens Are Tired of You

choices.text: Promise to die of old age

effects.log: "Good," the clerk says, and writes it down. Somehow you feel the promise settle into your bones. (+3 years)

choices.text: Ask for a copy of the stamp

effects.log: The clerk stamps the back of your hand. It fades by morning. Your luck does not.

choices.text: Thank the clerk for their patience

effects.log: The clerk pauses on the cloud. "Nobody ever thanks us," the clerk says, and goes up a little lighter.

events.text: The grey-robed clerk of the heavens sits down uninvited at your table and orders noodles. "So many," the clerk says. "We had a meeting about you. Some of us want to give you a medal. Some of us want to give you a different universe."

choices.text: Ask which way the vote went

effects.log: "A medal," the clerk says, "but we lost it." The noodles arrive. The clerk pays.

choices.text: Buy the clerk a second bowl

effects.log: Two bowls of noodles, one immortal official, many complaints about the heavens' office. A fine evening.

choices.text: Ask what lives they would choose

effects.log: The clerk thinks a long time. "A noodle seller," the clerk says. "Nobody files reports about noodles."

events.text: Golden light, and a ledger the size of a door opens in the sky over your house. Line after line, every one your name. At the bottom, a new line is being written as you watch. It does not say how you die. It only says: and again.

choices.text: Bow to the ledger

effects.log: The ledger closes with a sound like a temple bell. The whole village feels lighter for a week.

choices.text: Write your own line beneath it

ok.log: Your brush reaches the sky. One line, in your own hand. The heavens leave it there.

fail.log: Your brush cannot reach. The ledger closes, kindly, as if it understands the wish.

choices.text: Turn your back and go to work

effects.log: You have a field to plough. The ledger can wait. The heavens, for once, seem impressed.

events.text: The heavens have given up the paperwork. One morning a letter arrives, sealed in gold, delivered by a crane. It says only: WELCOME BACK. ASSUMED. NO NEED TO REPORT. It is signed by every clerk in the heavens, and a few of the signatures are small drawings of you.

choices.text: Frame the letter

effects.log: It hangs in your house all your life. Guests ask about it. You tell them it is a joke between old friends.

choices.text: Write back

effects.log: You write: THANK YOU. SEE YOU SOON. The crane takes it, looking pleased with itself.

choices.text: Feed the crane and let it stay

effects.log: The crane stays the whole life. When you die, it leaves first, to tell them you are coming.

events.text: In a crowd at the market, someone stops dead and looks at you. A stranger, any age, any face, and you know them at once, the way you know a scar. Another soul that keeps coming back. Across a dozen lives, you have been rivals, enemies, and once, very briefly, friends. They smile. "You again."

choices.text: Smile back. "You again."

effects.log: Two people grinning at each other in a fish market. Nobody else understands. You both prefer it that way.

choices.text: Walk away fast

effects.log: You hear them laughing behind you. They always find you anyway.

choices.text: Challenge them to a spar on the spot

effects.log: "Not here," they say. "The river bank. Dawn. Like the last time." You do not remember the last time. Your body does.

events.text: Dawn at the river bank. The other soul is already there, stretching. "Shall we keep score?" they ask. "I make it forty to thirty-eight, in my favour." You are sure it is the other way round.

choices.text: Spar in earnest

ok.log: You win, narrowly. "Forty to thirty-nine," you say. They insist it was a draw.

fail.log: They win, and help you up. "Forty-one," they say. You will remember the technique they used.

choices.text: Spar for fun, and not keep score

effects.log: The first fight in many lives with nothing on it. You both laugh too much to fight well.

choices.text: Sit on the bank and talk instead

effects.log: You compare notes on the heavens' clerks, the worst deaths, the best noodles. Nobody else alive could have this talk.

events.text: Word comes that the other soul has died, peacefully, old. A package has been left for you: a wooden practice sword, worn smooth in two different places, as if two different hands had held it over many lives. A note: Your turn to carry it. See you next time.

choices.text: Keep the practice sword

effects.log: You practise with it every morning. Sometimes your grip slips to the other worn place, and the form changes.

choices.text: Burn incense, and wait

effects.log: You light incense for a rival. Somewhere, someone just born is crying very loudly. You hope it is them.

choices.text: Write the score on the blade

effects.log: You write it carefully: a draw. They would argue. That is the whole point.

events.text: Another life, another face, and the same stubborn soul, now a child of ten who walks up and kicks you in the shin. "For the last time," the child says. "You know what you did." You do not. You probably deserve it.

choices.text: Kick back, gently

effects.log: The child laughs and runs off. The game is on again, for another lifetime.

choices.text: Bow and apologise, to be safe

effects.log: "Accepted," the child says grandly. "For now."

choices.text: Ask what you did

effects.log: "You know," the child says, and stalks away. You never find out. It will bother you for lives.

events.text: The other soul finds you on a mountain peak, grey-haired this time. "So many lives," they say, setting down two cups of wine. "I counted. We have never once both died old. Shall we try it, this time? Together?"

choices.text: Agree, and shake on it

effects.log: You shake on growing old. For once you both keep the promise. (+5 years)

choices.text: One last duel first, for old times

effects.log: A duel nobody watches, on a peak above the clouds. You both win. You both lose. You both laugh.

choices.text: Ask what they will do when it ends

effects.log: "It does not end," they say. "That is why it is worth doing well."

events.text: In a ruined library you find a book with no title. The first page begins: {echo_name} died at {echo_age}, of {echo_cause}. The next page is another life, and another. The ink is fresh. The last written page is yesterday, and it is about you.
events.arc: A Book of Your Other Lives

choices.text: Take the book with you

effects.log: It weighs almost nothing. You keep it wrapped in cloth and read a page each night.

choices.text: Read only the first page and close it

effects.log: One page is enough for now. You put it back on the shelf. The next day it is in your bag.

choices.text: Look for who is writing it

effects.log: Nobody in the ruin but you and a cat. The cat looks very innocent.

events.text: Each night the book adds a line about your day. It is never wrong. Tonight it reads: Tomorrow, at the bridge, the choice will matter. You do not know which bridge. There are four in town.
events.arc: A Book of Your Other Lives

choices.text: Go to all four bridges

effects.log: At the third, a child is about to fall from the rail. You catch them. The book that night says only: Good.

choices.text: Stay home, out of spite

effects.log: The book reads: Stayed home, out of spite. Then, in smaller letters: Fair.

choices.text: Write in the book yourself

ok.log: Your words stay. The book answers in the next line, politely, in the same hand.

fail.log: Your ink slides off the page like water off a leaf.

events.text: The book has reached its last page. It is blank except for one line: The rest is not written yet. Neither, you realise, are you.
events.arc: A Book of Your Other Lives

choices.text: Leave the last page empty

effects.log: You close it gently. Your life feels wider after that, as if a fence was taken down.

choices.text: Give the book to a temple library

effects.log: The librarians argue about it for years. It never writes again. Or never where they can see.

choices.text: Write one line: and again

effects.log: The ink stays. In some later life, you think, you will find this book again, and know your own hand.

events.text: A martial manual from the market has notes in the margins: corrections, jokes, a doodle of a frog. The hand is yours. The manual is two hundred years old. One note says: If you are reading this again, page forty is wrong.

choices.text: Turn to page forty

effects.log: Page forty is wrong. Your old note fixes it. The technique works beautifully.

choices.text: Add a note of your own

effects.log: You add: Thank you. Also, the frog is terrible. Some later self will laugh.

choices.text: Sell it on at a profit

effects.log: A collector pays well for annotated old manuals. You feel a little guilty about the frog. (+30 taels)

events.text: A hidden valley holds a library with a shelf for each of your lives, kept by librarians who do not age. The head librarian hands you a fresh, empty book. "For this one," the librarian says. "We find they write better if you hold the brush yourself."

choices.text: Take the brush and begin

effects.log: You write the first line of this life in your own hand. It is the best sentence you have ever written.

choices.text: Read the shelf of your first life

effects.log: One thin book. A short life, a small village, a kindness to a stranger. Everything since grew from it.

choices.text: Ask to work here for a while

effects.log: You dust your own lives for a season. It is humbling, and very funny in places.

events.text: A blind bard at a teahouse plays a song about a hero who keeps coming back. The details are all wrong. Then, in the middle of a verse, the bard stops, turns toward you, and says, "Ah. Here is the hero now. Sit closer. I have been singing about you for a very long time."
events.arc: The Bard Who Sings of You

choices.text: Sit closer

effects.log: The bard plays the next verse just for you. It is about a death you had forgotten. You cry, a little, into your tea.

choices.text: Say the bard has the wrong person

effects.log: "Of course," the bard says, smiling. "Everyone says that the first time."

choices.text: Correct the details of the song

effects.log: The bard listens closely, nodding. "Better," the bard says. "But mine scans."

events.text: The bard asks for your help. "I am writing the new verse," the bard says. "Yours. The one you are living. But I need to know: is it a song of glory, of love, or of a quiet life?" Every listener in the teahouse leans in.
events.arc: The Bard Who Sings of You

choices.text: Glory

effects.log: The bard plays a fanfare on one string. The teahouse cheers. You will have to live up to it now.

choices.text: Love

effects.log: A slow verse, and half the teahouse goes home to someone. The bard looks smug.

choices.text: A quiet life

effects.log: The bard plays almost nothing, and the room goes still. It is the most beautiful verse of the night.

events.text: The bard is dying, very old, in a room above the teahouse. "I sang you in every life," the bard whispers. "Every life. Every bard. We pass you down, singer to singer. Will you sing for me, this once?"
events.arc: The Bard Who Sings of You

choices.text: Sing the bard a song

effects.log: You sing badly, and the bard laughs, and then is quiet, and smiling. The song goes on from you now.

choices.text: Take up the zither and learn it

effects.log: You learn the hundred verses in a season. The last one you write yourself.

choices.text: Promise the song will not end

effects.log: "It cannot," the bard says. "You keep coming back to give it new verses."

events.text: Street children are acting out the Ballad of the Returning Hero with sticks. In their version you died fighting a dragon. One of your real deaths, in fact, was falling off a roof while chasing a hat. The children are having a wonderful time.

choices.text: Join in as the dragon

effects.log: You are slain magnificently, many times, to cheering. Much better than the hat.

choices.text: Tell them about the hat

effects.log: They do not believe you. One of them, years later, becomes a bard and puts the hat in. It is the best verse.

choices.text: Watch, and say nothing

effects.log: Let them have the dragon. Nobody needs to know about the hat.

events.text: Every bard in the province comes to one teahouse on one night to sing the newest verse of the Returning Hero. Nobody knows it is about you. You sit in the back with a bowl of noodles as a hundred voices sing your lives into one long song.

choices.text: Stay to the end, unknown

effects.log: The last note fades. Nobody turns around. It is the most private glory a soul could have.

choices.text: Stand and sing the last verse

ok.log: Your voice is not good. It does not matter. The teahouse knows the song is true.

fail.log: Your voice cracks on the high note. The bards cheer anyway. They always did.

choices.text: Pay for every bard's wine (40 taels)

effects.log: A hundred bards drinking to a hero they cannot see. They toast you anyway, by accident. (-40 taels)
